title: "One day of traffic: 2026-09-30"
date: 2026-10-01

::: {.callout-note}
## A dated snapshot
These numbers describe one full UTC day, 2026-09-30, two days after the cutover, for <!-- docs-check: ok -->
bioconductor.org and www.bioconductor.org. They are measurements, not trends, and this page will
not be updated. They come from the request logs in bioc-traffic (one record per request,
delivered by Logpush; see [ADR 0003](adr/0003-request-logging-after-the-cloudflare-cutover.md)),
queried with DuckDB through its `access` and `downloads` views and its first-pass (v0) traffic
classification ([bioc-traffic#5](https://github.com/seandavi/bioc-traffic/issues/5)).
Where something is an estimate or an unchecked assumption, it says so.
:::

## The day at a glance

| | |
|---|---:|
| Requests | 5.8M |
| Bytes served | 8.1 TB |
| Countries | 215 |
| Distinct client addresses (hashed) | 723,948 |
| Distinct R installations (addresses sending R's user agent) | about 21,000 |
| Busiest hour | 09:00 UTC, 388,115 requests |
| Served from the edge cache | 48.7% of requests, 22% of bytes |

"Installations" and "clients" are distinct hashed addresses, not people. One address can be a
whole university behind NAT, and one person can use several.

| v0 class | Requests | Share | Distinct addresses |

| R and package clients | 1.89M | 32.6% | 35,974 |

"Other automation" is v0's `likely_automated` class, and it is mostly machines in clouds
presenting browser user agents:

| Why v0 called it automated | Requests | Share | Distinct addresses |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Browser user agent carrying `gzip(gfe)`, which Google's front end appends to requests from Google Cloud | 995,257 | 52.8% | 737 |
| Browser user agent from a hosting or cloud network (Google Cloud, RapidSeedbox, Datacamp, Azure, AWS, Alibaba lead) | 703,442 | 37.3% | 182,316 |
| HTTP libraries (Go, Java, Node and others) | 58,189 | 3.1% | 178 |
| Headless browsers and scrapers | 38,281 | 2.0% | 19,459 |
| curl | 32,869 | 1.7% | 4,725 |
| Other self-declared bots | 20,915 | 1.1% | 3,859 |
| Python | 12,458 | 0.7% | 524 |
| Everything else (fake browser strings, verified fetchers, no user agent, scanner paths, HEAD from a browser) | 24,517 | 1.3% | |

48% of these requests were for build reports and 42% for `/packages/`. The rules are in
bioc-traffic's [`sql/client_class.sql`](https://github.com/seandavi/bioc-traffic/blob/main/sql/client_class.sql); a browser on a VPN that exits through a hosting network
lands here too, which is a known limit of v0.

"Browser-like" is deliberately not called "humans". By distinct address it is led by Vietnam
(83,053), China (55,337), the US (54,453) and Brazil (49,013). That looks like crawlers on
residential connections, which v0 does not yet separate out. The 42,514 unknown requests
fetched 902 GB.

## R clients

- About 1.0M requests came from 20,966 distinct R installations.
- By R version: 4.6 is 56%, 4.5 23%, 4.4 15%, 4.3 6%, 4.1 5%, and 4.7 (devel) 3%.
- By OS: Linux 12,347, Windows 6,303, macOS 2,650.
- 24,836 distinct clients fetched `config.yaml`, which BiocManager reads to check versions.
- R clients made 400,509 package downloads from 12,463 distinct addresses. Software packages
  were 95.7% of them, annotation data 3.4%, experiment data 0.6%, and workflows 27 downloads.
  The most downloaded were BiocVersion, S4Vectors, BiocGenerics, SparseArray and IRanges.

**One machine made 162,163 downloads of Bioconductor 3.19 packages,** 40% of everything R
clients downloaded that day. That is almost certainly a script reinstalling in a loop. The
legacy download statistics would have counted every one, which is why the
[download stats](download-stats.qmd) need classification before they mean anything.

## Build reports

`/checkResults/` took 1,273,130 requests (22% of all requests) from 241,607 distinct addresses.
Some of that is maintainers reading their build logs; much of it is crawlers walking the
reports, which are a long tail of pages that change daily.

## Why the edge cache hit rate is only 49%

48.7% of requests and 22% of bytes came from the edge cache. That matters less than it
sounds. R2 charges nothing for data transfer, so a miss costs one storage read, about $0.36 per
million at list price. At about 2.6M misses a day that is on the order of $30 a month (an
estimate, not a bill). The real cost of a miss is latency: earlier measurements put it at about
200 ms in the western US and 650–800 ms from Europe and Asia. Four causes, measured:

**1. Half the misses could never have been hits.** 49% of misses were the first request for
that URL anywhere that day, and 59% of URLs were requested only once. The worst classes are
long tails that crawlers walk; the files installs depend on are cached well:

| Path type | Requests | Hit rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Build reports (`checkResults/`) | 1.27M | 13% |
| Package landing pages | 465k | 12% |
| Repository indexes (`PACKAGES*`, `VIEWS`, `config.yaml`) | 1.1M | 91% (98% of bytes) |
| Site assets | 930k | 82% |
| Package files | 804k | 53% |

**2. The cache is per data centre.** Requests came through 256 Cloudflare data centres, and
the Worker's cache (the Cache API) is local to each one. 32% of misses were for a URL already
cached in another data centre that day. Our understanding, not yet checked, is that
Cloudflare's tiered caching does not apply to the Cache API; serving through Cloudflare's own
cache instead would pick it up.

**3. Files over 512 MB are never cached.** About 2,800 requests for 841 such files fetched
3.5 TB, 43% of all bytes served, with 7 cache hits. They are annotation and experiment data:
BSgenome hg38/hg19/mm10, the dbSNP155 SNPlocs packages (6 GB each), MafDb. 512 MB is, as we
understand it, Cloudflare's per-object cache limit; we have not verified that. This alone is
why the byte hit rate is so far below the request hit rate. (One query first counted 45,357
requests for these files; two narrower queries agree on about 2,800, and the 3.5 TB total is
the same in all three.)

**4. The rest, 18.5% of misses,** were repeats in the same data centre: eviction, the hourly
sync's purges, and 404s that had expired.

## Should 404s be cached longer?

There were 1.09M 404 responses: 471k from the cache and 601k misses. 404s are cached for ten
minutes, keyed by path and build ([Edge cache](cache.qmd)). Grouping each miss by the time since
the last 404 for the same URL in the same data centre:

| 404 miss | Count | Would a longer TTL have saved it? |
|---|---:|---|
| First for that URL in that data centre that day | 419k | No |
| Within 10 minutes (evicted early) | 40k | No |
| 10–60 minutes later | 69k | Yes, at 1 h |
| 1–6 hours later | 64k | Yes, at 6 h |
| More than 6 hours later | 9k | Yes, at 24 h |

A 6-hour TTL would have removed about 133k of 601k misses (22%), worth very roughly $5 a month
in storage reads (an estimate), and the latency saved goes mostly to crawlers and probes. The
risk is that the hourly sync purges by object key, so it never clears a cached 404. A package
published on master would keep 404ing for up to the TTL in every data centre that asked for it
just before. At ten minutes that is harmless; at six hours an install right after an
announcement could fail for an afternoon. So the TTL stays at ten minutes unless sync.sh first
learns to purge the 404 entries for newly added keys.
